title: A Surveillance ‘Cat-and-Mouse’ Game With AI
excerpt: Is there any way of fighting back?
content_html:
Anthony “Bingy” Arillotta waited years to become a made man in the Genovese crime family, and when at last the call came in August 2003, he followed directions to the letter. According to sworn testimony, Arillotta was summoned to a steak house in the Bronx, where he was made to hand over his cellphone, beeper, and jewelry before being driven to an apartment building. When he got there, he was taken to a small bathroom and strip-searched for electronic devices. For his big meeting with the boss, he was given a bathrobe to wear.

Until recently, only spies and criminals had to worry this obsessively about their private statements being picked up by electronic equipment. But soon, the average person might need to deploy surveillance countermeasures. The next time you conduct a delicate bit of office diplomacy or share a romantic or financial secret with a friend over drinks, a sensor built into someone’s glasses, necklace, or lapel pin might be watching you and listening.

In March, the tech start-up Deveillance announced the development of Spectre I, a hockey-puck-shaped device that purports to prevent others from recording you (no strip search required). The company was founded by Aida Baradari, a recent college graduate who was worried by the surge in people wearing AI-enabled recorders. These wearables can be used as a silent notetaker, a personal assistant, or even a therapist of sorts. That technology isn’t yet mainstream, but it may be soon. Apple—the company with the largest personal-tech ecosystem in the world—is rumored to be developing an AI pin or pendant that would serve as an iPhone’s constant eyes and ears; many other products of this type are on the way. AI accessories could one day be as widespread as AirPods.

New surveillance technologies tend to breed new countermeasures, which lead, in turn, to more sophisticated surveillance. During the Second World War, after Germany operationalized radar, the Royal Air Force began dropping thin strips of metallized paper cut to a specific size that resonated with the radar, swamping German screens with phantom echoes that were indistinguishable from real aircraft. Some historians have argued that the ensuing radar arms race was more consequential to the war’s outcome than the Manhattan Project.

For decades, crude jammers have been sold to people who hope to avoid being recorded. Early versions blasted loud, unpleasant white noise to conceal voices. More recently, companies have made models that emit a steady stream of ultrasonic sound at inaudible frequencies, exploiting a quirk of microphone hardware that converts those high frequencies into noise. In 2020, a team at the University of Chicago led by Yuxin Chen reported that it had mounted 23 ultrasonic transducers on a single bracelet, such that jamming signals could be sent in all directions instead of being focused on a single target.

But even high-tech jammers have a hard time fending off today’s AI wearables. The most advanced pins, pendants, and glasses use speech-recovery algorithms to strip away unwanted noise, whether it originates from everyday sources—such as the clinking of glasses in a crowded bar—or from an ultrasonic jammer. This task the algorithms perform is quite difficult: In that crowded bar, a microphone on a person’s lapel will intercept sound vibrations from many different sources at once. It will pick up a bartender calling out a drink order, music emanating from a speaker, bursts of laughter coming from nearby tables—and all of these sounds ricochet off of walls and other objects, creating yet more noise. The human body solves this “cocktail party problem” without us noticing: Our ears serve as dual microphones, and our brain can use the timing and intensity differences between them, along with layered processing in the auditory cortex, to isolate the voice of a person who is sitting across from us.

DeLiang Wang, a computer scientist at Ohio State University, has spent decades training neural networks to accomplish that same goal, for the purpose of improving hearing aids. By feeding the networks hundreds of hours of recorded human voices, he has taught them to recognize the frequencies and rhythms of speech. The models build an internal representation of “speech-ness,” and when they encounter a noisy recording, they focus on the parts that match the patterns they have learned and then suppress everything else. The most advanced technologies can now infer missing syllables in the way that a reader fills in a redacted word from context, allowing them to reconstruct speech that wasn’t cleanly captured in the first place.

Big tech companies are trying to do this too. Microsoft has been running an annual Deep Noise Suppression Challenge since 2020 to advance the field. (Their in-house team is trying to make Teams meetings less excruciating.) Other companies are working on noise cancellation for cellphone calls and podcast software. This sort of research is meant to improve the lives of normal users of technology—assuming that we podcast listeners count as normal—but every advance in de-noising can also be used to help an AI assistant recover speech from a jammed recording.

Defeating these algorithms may require a different countersurveillance approach altogether. Finn Brunton, a historian at UC Davis and the co-author of Obfuscation: A User’s Guide for Privacy and Protest, told me that one of the best ways is to identify the data that a device is trying to collect, and then supply it with a junk version. The Berlin-based artist Adam Harvey used this strategy when he developed makeup and clothing that frustrate facial-recognition algorithms. Daniel Howe and Helen Nissenbaum did something similar with a browser plug-in called TrackMeNot: Rather than concealing a user’s Google searches, the extension continually runs its own randomized decoy queries in the background, so that whatever a user actually searched for becomes lost in a sea of false leads.

People have tried this technique in the realm of audio too. Woodrow Hartzog, a law professor at Boston University who studies privacy and surveillance, told me that early in his legal career, he worked with defense attorneys who worried that their jailhouse conversations with clients would be recorded. To fight back, they played “babble tapes”—audio files layered with 40 tracks of voices in different accents—in the background.

In 2023, a team led by Ming Gao, now a researcher at Nanjing University, used human voices to defeat speech-recovery algorithms in a different way. Its jammer, called MicFrozen, is worn by a speaker who doesn’t want to be recorded. It listens as they talk and then generates a real-time stream of ultrasonic “anti-speech” tuned to the speaker’s voice, much like the noise-cancellation technology in your headphones. The device then sends out another layer of counterfeit speech-shaped sound to mislead any algorithm that tries to reconstruct what was lost.

Baradari, whose company is working on the Spectre I device, wouldn’t tell me exactly how her jammer’s signals work, but she said that they, too, resemble speech. The launch video for Spectre I claims that the device will also be able to detect the presence of nearby microphones. When I asked Baradari how it will do that, she clarified that her team is still “working on that part right now.”

However effective Spectre I turns out to be, it won’t be the end of the recording arms race. More capable AI models may eventually deploy some new listening tricks of their own. They may bypass recorded audio altogether. In Stanley Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey, when two astronauts retreat to a soundproofed pod to discuss disconnecting HAL 9000, the ship’s computer simply reads their lips through the porthole. A wearable powered by a model that’s been trained on enough conversation footage could, in principle, do the same. In theory, it could also stare at a glass of water between two people and recover their speech from vibrations on the liquid’s surface.

AI wearables may always have an edge over countermeasures. After all, they’re using a technology that is a product of the entire speech-processing industry, which takes in billions of dollars in investments—not just for AI assistants but also for hearing aids, smart speakers, and teleconferencing tools. Meanwhile, only a few academics and small companies are defending us from these technologies. “The thing about cat-and-mouse games is that we know how they usually end up for the mouse,” Hartzog said. “And in this case, the cat includes some of the most powerful corporations to ever exist.”

The Mafia knows what it’s like to be a mouse. By the time Arillotta, the aspiring made man, was told to put on the bathrobe, criminal organizations had been engaged in surveillance arms races of their own for decades. After law enforcement started bugging their phones, bosses would conduct business in person. Sometimes, they’d use a safe house or a vehicle, but those could be bugged, too, and so sensitive information might have been communicated only during a walk-and-talk. Eventually, crime families turned to burner phones, and then devices with encryption. But here, again, they fell prey to the cat.

In 2018, the FBI began secretly running Anom, its own encrypted-phone company. Through informants, it sold 12,000 devices with a special Anom messaging app. Members of Mafia families, motorcycle gangs, and other criminal organizations treated the phones as a status symbol, and used them to negotiate drug deals, launder money, and participate in all manner of other illegal activity. But the security that they offered was a ruse: Every message that they sent was being intercepted by the feds.

By feeding the networks hundreds of hours of recorded human voices, he has taught them to recognize the frequencies and rhythms of speech. The models build an internal representation of “speech-ness,” and when they encounter a noisy recording, they focus on the parts that match the patterns they have learned and then suppress everything else. The most advanced technologies can now infer missing syllables in the way that a reader fills in a redacted word from context, allowing them to reconstruct speech that wasn’t cleanly captured in the first place.

sentences.en: DeLiang Wang, a computer scientist at Ohio State University, has spent decades training neural networks to accomplish that same goal, for the purpose of improving hearing aids.
sentences.zh: DeLiang Wang 是俄亥俄州立大学的计算机科学家，他花了几十年的时间训练神经网络来实现同样的目标，以改善助听器。

sentences.en: By feeding the networks hundreds of hours of recorded human voices, he has taught them to recognize the frequencies and rhythms of speech.
sentences.zh: 通过向网络提供数百小时录制的人类声音，他教会了它们识别语音的频率和节奏。

sentences.en: The models build an internal representation of “speech-ness,” and when they encounter a noisy recording, they focus on the parts that match the patterns they have learned and then suppress everything else.
sentences.zh: 这些模型构建了“言语性”的内部表征，当它们遇到嘈杂的录音时，它们会专注于与所学模式相匹配的部分，然后抑制其他所有内容。

sentences.en: The most advanced technologies can now infer missing syllables in the way that a reader fills in a redacted word from context, allowing them to reconstruct speech that wasn’t cleanly captured in the first place.
sentences.zh: 现在，最先进的技术可以通过读者根据上下文填写经过编辑的单词来推断缺失的音节，从而使他们能够重建最初没有清晰捕获的语音。

blocks.html_en: Big tech companies are trying to do this too. Microsoft has been running an annual Deep Noise Suppression Challenge since 2020 to advance the field. (Their in-house team is trying to make Teams meetings less excruciating.) Other companies are working on noise cancellation for cellphone calls and podcast software. This sort of research is meant to improve the lives of normal users of technology—assuming that we podcast listeners count as normal—but every advance in de-noising can also be used to help an AI assistant recover speech from a jammed recording.

sentences.en: Big tech companies are trying to do this too.
sentences.zh: 大型科技公司也在尝试这样做。

sentences.en: Microsoft has been running an annual Deep Noise Suppression Challenge since 2020 to advance the field.
sentences.zh: 自 2020 年以来，微软一直在举办年度深度噪声抑制挑战赛，以推动该领域的发展。

sentences.en: (Their in-house team is trying to make Teams meetings less excruciating.)
sentences.zh: （他们的内部团队正在努力让 Teams 会议变得不那么痛苦。）

sentences.en: Other companies are working on noise cancellation for cellphone calls and podcast software.
sentences.zh: 其他公司正在致力于手机通话和播客软件的噪音消除。

sentences.en: This sort of research is meant to improve the lives of normal users of technology—assuming that we podcast listeners count as normal—but every advance in de-noising can also be used to help an AI assistant recover speech from a jammed recording.
sentences.zh: 这类研究的目的是改善普通技术用户的生活——假设我们播客听众算正常——但去噪方面的每一项进步也可以用来帮助人工智能助手从堵塞的录音中恢复语音。

blocks.html_en: Defeating these algorithms may require a different countersurveillance approach altogether. Finn Brunton, a historian at UC Davis and the co-author of Obfuscation: A User’s Guide for Privacy and Protest, told me that one of the best ways is to identify the data that a device is trying to collect, and then supply it with a junk version. The Berlin-based artist Adam Harvey used this strategy when he developed makeup and clothing that frustrate facial-recognition algorithms. Daniel Howe and Helen Nissenbaum did something similar with a browser plug-in called TrackMeNot: Rather than concealing a user’s Google searches, the extension continually runs its own randomized decoy queries in the background, so that whatever a user actually searched for becomes lost in a sea of false leads.

sentences.en: Defeating these algorithms may require a different countersurveillance approach altogether.
sentences.zh: 击败这些算法可能需要完全不同的反监视方法。

sentences.en: Finn Brunton, a historian at UC Davis and the co-author of Obfuscation: A User’s Guide for Privacy and Protest, told me that one of the best ways is to identify the data that a device is trying to collect, and then supply it with a junk version.
sentences.zh: 加州大学戴维斯分校的历史学家、《混淆：隐私和抗议用户指南》的合著者 Finn Brunton 告诉我，最好的方法之一是识别设备试图收集的数据，然后向其提供垃圾版本。

sentences.en: The Berlin-based artist Adam Harvey used this strategy when he developed makeup and clothing that frustrate facial-recognition algorithms.
sentences.zh: 柏林艺术家 Adam Harvey 在开发阻碍面部识别算法的化妆品和服装时就使用了这一策略。

sentences.en: Daniel Howe and Helen Nissenbaum did something similar with a browser plug-in called TrackMeNot: Rather than concealing a user’s Google searches, the extension continually runs its own randomized decoy queries in the background, so that whatever a user actually searched for becomes lost in a sea of false leads.
sentences.zh: Daniel Howe 和 Helen Nissenbaum 对名为 TrackMeNot 的浏览器插件做了类似的事情：该扩展程序不是隐藏用户的 Google 搜索，而是在后台不断运行自己的随机诱饵查询，因此用户实际搜索的任何内容都会迷失在虚假线索的海洋中。

blocks.html_en: People have tried this technique in the realm of audio too. Woodrow Hartzog, a law professor at Boston University who studies privacy and surveillance, told me that early in his legal career, he worked with defense attorneys who worried that their jailhouse conversations with clients would be recorded. To fight back, they played “babble tapes”—audio files layered with 40 tracks of voices in different accents—in the background.

sentences.en: People have tried this technique in the realm of audio too.
sentences.zh: 人们也在音频领域尝试过这种技术。

sentences.en: Woodrow Hartzog, a law professor at Boston University who studies privacy and surveillance, told me that early in his legal career, he worked with defense attorneys who worried that their jailhouse conversations with clients would be recorded.
sentences.zh: 波士顿大学研究隐私和监控的法学教授伍德罗·哈佐格 (Woodrow Hartzog) 告诉我，在他的法律职业生涯早期，他与辩护律师合作，他们担心他们与客户的监狱谈话会被记录。

sentences.en: To fight back, they played “babble tapes”—audio files layered with 40 tracks of voices in different accents—in the background.
sentences.zh: 为了反击，他们在后台播放了“胡言乱语磁带”——由 40 首不同口音的声音分层组成的音频文件。

blocks.html_en: In 2023, a team led by Ming Gao, now a researcher at Nanjing University, used human voices to defeat speech-recovery algorithms in a different way. Its jammer, called MicFrozen, is worn by a speaker who doesn’t want to be recorded. It listens as they talk and then generates a real-time stream of ultrasonic “anti-speech” tuned to the speaker’s voice, much like the noise-cancellation technology in your headphones. The device then sends out another layer of counterfeit speech-shaped sound to mislead any algorithm that tries to reconstruct what was lost.

sentences.en: In 2023, a team led by Ming Gao, now a researcher at Nanjing University, used human voices to defeat speech-recovery algorithms in a different way.
sentences.zh: 2023年，南京大学研究员高明领导的团队利用人声以不同的方式击败了语音恢复算法。

sentences.en: Its jammer, called MicFrozen, is worn by a speaker who doesn’t want to be recorded.
sentences.zh: 它的干扰器名为 MicFrozen，由不想被录音的演讲者佩戴。

sentences.en: It listens as they talk and then generates a real-time stream of ultrasonic “anti-speech” tuned to the speaker’s voice, much like the noise-cancellation technology in your headphones.
sentences.zh: 它会在他们说话时进行监听，然后根据说话者的声音生成实时超声波“反语音”流，就像耳机中的降噪技术一样。

sentences.en: The device then sends out another layer of counterfeit speech-shaped sound to mislead any algorithm that tries to reconstruct what was lost.
sentences.zh: 然后，该设备发出另一层伪造的语音形状的声音，以误导任何试图重建丢失内容的算法。

blocks.html_en: Baradari, whose company is working on the Spectre I device, wouldn’t tell me exactly how her jammer’s signals work, but she said that they, too, resemble speech. The launch video for Spectre I claims that the device will also be able to detect the presence of nearby microphones. When I asked Baradari how it will do that, she clarified that her team is still “working on that part right now.”

sentences.en: Baradari, whose company is working on the Spectre I device, wouldn’t tell me exactly how her jammer’s signals work, but she said that they, too, resemble speech.
sentences.zh: 巴拉达里的公司正在研发 Spectre I 设备，她不愿告诉我她的干扰器信号是如何工作的，但她说它们也类似于语音。

sentences.en: The launch video for Spectre I claims that the device will also be able to detect the presence of nearby microphones.
sentences.zh: Spectre I 的发布视频声称该设备还能够检测附近麦克风的存在。

sentences.en: When I asked Baradari how it will do that, she clarified that her team is still “working on that part right now.”
sentences.zh: 当我问巴拉达里将如何做到这一点时，她澄清说她的团队“目前仍在研究这部分内容”。

blocks.html_en: However effective Spectre I turns out to be, it won’t be the end of the recording arms race. More capable AI models may eventually deploy some new listening tricks of their own. They may bypass recorded audio altogether. In Stanley Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey, when two astronauts retreat to a soundproofed pod to discuss disconnecting HAL 9000, the ship’s computer simply reads their lips through the porthole. A wearable powered by a model that’s been trained on enough conversation footage could, in principle, do the same. In theory, it could also stare at a glass of water between two people and recover their speech from vibrations on the liquid’s surface.

sentences.en: However effective Spectre I turns out to be, it won’t be the end of the recording arms race.
sentences.zh: 无论《Spectre I》的效果如何，录音军备竞赛都不会结束。

sentences.en: More capable AI models may eventually deploy some new listening tricks of their own.
sentences.zh: 更强大的人工智能模型最终可能会部署一些自己的新聆听技巧。

sentences.en: They may bypass recorded audio altogether.
sentences.zh: 他们可能会完全绕过录制的音频。

sentences.en: In Stanley Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey, when two astronauts retreat to a soundproofed pod to discuss disconnecting HAL 9000, the ship’s computer simply reads their lips through the porthole.
sentences.zh: 在斯坦利·库布里克的《2001：太空漫游》中，当两名宇航员退回隔音舱讨论断开 HAL 9000 的连接时，飞船上的计算机只是通过舷窗读取他们的嘴唇信息。

sentences.en: A wearable powered by a model that’s been trained on enough conversation footage could, in principle, do the same.
sentences.zh: 原则上，由经过足够对话镜头训练的模型驱动的可穿戴设备也可以做到同样的事情。

sentences.en: In theory, it could also stare at a glass of water between two people and recover their speech from vibrations on the liquid’s surface.
sentences.zh: 理论上，它还可以盯着两个人之间的一杯水，并从液体表面的振动中恢复他们的语言。

blocks.html_en: AI wearables may always have an edge over countermeasures. After all, they’re using a technology that is a product of the entire speech-processing industry, which takes in billions of dollars in investments—not just for AI assistants but also for hearing aids, smart speakers, and teleconferencing tools. Meanwhile, only a few academics and small companies are defending us from these technologies. “The thing about cat-and-mouse games is that we know how they usually end up for the mouse,” Hartzog said. “And in this case, the cat includes some of the most powerful corporations to ever exist.”

sentences.en: AI wearables may always have an edge over countermeasures.
sentences.zh: 人工智能可穿戴设备可能总是比对抗措施更具优势。

sentences.en: After all, they’re using a technology that is a product of the entire speech-processing industry, which takes in billions of dollars in investments—not just for AI assistants but also for hearing aids, smart speakers, and teleconferencing tools.
sentences.zh: 毕竟，他们使用的技术是整个语音处理行业的产物，该行业需要数十亿美元的投资——不仅用于人工智能助理，还用于助听器、智能扬声器和电话会议工具。

sentences.en: Meanwhile, only a few academics and small companies are defending us from these technologies.
sentences.zh: 与此同时，只有少数学者和小公司在保护我们免受这些技术的侵害。

sentences.en: “The thing about cat-and-mouse games is that we know how they usually end up for the mouse,” Hartzog said.
sentences.zh: “猫捉老鼠游戏的特点是，我们知道它们通常会如何落入老鼠手中，”哈佐格说。

sentences.en: “And in this case, the cat includes some of the most powerful corporations to ever exist.”
sentences.zh: “在这种情况下，这只猫包括一些有史以来最强大的公司。”

blocks.html_en: The Mafia knows what it’s like to be a mouse. By the time Arillotta, the aspiring made man, was told to put on the bathrobe, criminal organizations had been engaged in surveillance arms races of their own for decades. After law enforcement started bugging their phones, bosses would conduct business in person. Sometimes, they’d use a safe house or a vehicle, but those could be bugged, too, and so sensitive information might have been communicated only during a walk-and-talk. Eventually, crime families turned to burner phones, and then devices with encryption. But here, again, they fell prey to the cat.

sentences.en: The Mafia knows what it’s like to be a mouse.
sentences.zh: 黑手党知道当一只老鼠是什么感觉。

sentences.en: By the time Arillotta, the aspiring made man, was told to put on the bathrobe, criminal organizations had been engaged in surveillance arms races of their own for decades.
sentences.zh: 当阿里洛塔这个有抱负的男人被告知穿上浴袍时，犯罪组织已经进行了数十年的监视军备竞赛。

sentences.en: After law enforcement started bugging their phones, bosses would conduct business in person.
sentences.zh: 执法部门开始窃听他们的电话后，老板们就会亲自处理业务。

sentences.en: Sometimes, they’d use a safe house or a vehicle, but those could be bugged, too, and so sensitive information might have been communicated only during a walk-and-talk.
sentences.zh: 有时，他们会使用安全屋或车辆，但这些也可能被窃听，因此敏感信息可能只能在边走边说的过程中传达。

sentences.en: Eventually, crime families turned to burner phones, and then devices with encryption.
sentences.zh: 最终，犯罪家族转向一次性手机，然后是加密设备。

sentences.en: But here, again, they fell prey to the cat.
sentences.zh: 但在这里，他们再次成为猫的牺牲品。

blocks.html_en: In 2018, the FBI began secretly running Anom, its own encrypted-phone company. Through informants, it sold 12,000 devices with a special Anom messaging app. Members of Mafia families, motorcycle gangs, and other criminal organizations treated the phones as a status symbol, and used them to negotiate drug deals, launder money, and participate in all manner of other illegal activity. But the security that they offered was a ruse: Every message that they sent was being intercepted by the feds.

sentences.en: In 2018, the FBI began secretly running Anom, its own encrypted-phone company.
sentences.zh: 2018 年，FBI 开始秘密运营自己的加密电话公司 Anom。

sentences.en: Through informants, it sold 12,000 devices with a special Anom messaging app.
sentences.zh: 通过线人，该公司销售了 12,000 台带有特殊 Anom 消息应用程序的设备。

sentences.en: Members of Mafia families, motorcycle gangs, and other criminal organizations treated the phones as a status symbol, and used them to negotiate drug deals, launder money, and participate in all manner of other illegal activity.
sentences.zh: 黑手党家庭、摩托车团伙和其他犯罪组织的成员将手机视为身份象征，并用它们来谈判毒品交易、洗钱以及参与各种其他非法活动。

sentences.en: But the security that they offered was a ruse: Every message that they sent was being intercepted by the feds.
sentences.zh: 但他们提供的安全措施是一个诡计：他们发送的每条消息都被联邦政府拦截。

content_html_zh:
安东尼·“宾吉”·阿里洛塔（Anthony“Bingy”Arillotta）等待了数年，才成为吉诺维斯犯罪家族的一员，当 2003 年 8 月终于接到电话时，他按照信中的指示行事。 根据宣誓证词，阿里洛塔被传唤到布朗克斯的一家牛排馆，在那里他被要求交出手机、传呼机和珠宝，然后被送往一栋公寓楼。 当他到达那里时，他被带到一个小浴室，并脱衣搜查电子设备。 在与老板的大型会议上，他们给了他一件浴袍。

直到最近，只有间谍和犯罪分子才不得不担心他们的私人陈述被电子设备窃取。 但很快，普通人可能需要部署监视对策。 下次当你进行微妙的办公室外交或与朋友喝酒时分享浪漫或财务秘密时，内置在某人眼镜、项链或翻领别针中的传感器可能会监视你并倾听你的声音。

今年 3 月，科技初创公司 Deveillance 宣布开发出 Spectre I，这是一款曲棍球形状的设备，旨在防止他人对您进行录音（无需脱衣搜查）。 该公司由刚毕业的大学毕业生艾达·巴拉达里 (Aida Baradari) 创立，她对佩戴人工智能录音机的人数激增感到担忧。 这些可穿戴设备可以用作无声记事员、私人助理，甚至是某种治疗师。 该技术尚未成为主流，但可能很快就会成为主流。 据传，苹果公司——拥有世界上最大的个人科技生态系统的公司——正在开发一款人工智能别针或吊坠，作为 iPhone 的持续眼睛和耳朵；许多其他此类产品正在开发中。 人工智能配件有一天可能会像 AirPods 一样普及。

新的监控技术往往会催生新的对策，进而导致更复杂的监控。 第二次世界大战期间，德国投入使用雷达后，英国皇家空军开始投放切成特定尺寸的金属化纸细条，与雷达产生共振，使德国屏幕上充满了与真实飞机无法区分的幻影回声。 一些历史学家认为，随之而来的雷达军备竞赛对战争结果的影响比曼哈顿计划更为重要。

几十年来，粗制滥造的干扰器一直被卖给那些希望避免被录音的人。 早期版本会发出响亮、令人不快的白噪音来掩盖声音。 最近，一些公司制作了能够以听不见的频率发出稳定的超声波流的模型，利用麦克风硬件的一个特性将这些高频转换为噪声。 2020年，芝加哥大学陈宇鑫领导的团队报告称，他们在一个手环上安装了23个超声波换能器，这样干扰信号就可以向各个方向发送，而不是集中在单个目标上。

阅读：纽约最受谩骂的科技首席执行官直面他的仇恨者

但即使是高科技干扰器也很难抵御当今的人工智能可穿戴设备。 最先进的别针、吊坠和眼镜使用语音恢复算法来消除不需要的噪音，无论这些噪音是来自日常来源（例如拥挤的酒吧中玻璃杯的叮当声）还是来自超声波干扰器。 算法执行的这项任务相当困难：在那个拥挤的酒吧里，一个人翻领上的麦克风会同时拦截来自许多不同来源的声音振动。 它会听到调酒师喊出饮料单、扬声器发出的音乐、附近桌子上传来的阵阵笑声——所有这些声音都会从墙壁和其他物体上反弹，产生更多噪音。 人体在我们没有注意到的情况下解决了这个“鸡尾酒会问题”：我们的耳朵充当双麦克风，我们的大脑可以利用它们之间的时间和强度差异，以及听觉皮层的分层处理，来隔离坐在我们对面的人的声音。

DeLiang Wang 是俄亥俄州立大学的计算机科学家，他花了几十年的时间训练神经网络来实现同样的目标，以改善助听器。 通过向网络提供数百小时录制的人类声音，他教会了它们识别语音的频率和节奏。 这些模型构建了“言语性”的内部表征，当它们遇到嘈杂的录音时，它们会专注于与所学模式相匹配的部分，然后抑制其他所有内容。 现在，最先进的技术可以通过读者根据上下文填写经过编辑的单词来推断缺失的音节，从而使他们能够重建最初没有清晰捕获的语音。

大型科技公司也在尝试这样做。 自 2020 年以来，微软一直在举办年度深度噪声抑制挑战赛，以推动该领域的发展。 （他们的内部团队正在努力让 Teams 会议变得不那么痛苦。） 其他公司正在致力于手机通话和播客软件的噪音消除。 这类研究的目的是改善普通技术用户的生活——假设我们播客听众算正常——但去噪方面的每一项进步也可以用来帮助人工智能助手从堵塞的录音中恢复语音。

击败这些算法可能需要完全不同的反监视方法。 加州大学戴维斯分校的历史学家、《混淆：隐私和抗议用户指南》的合著者 Finn Brunton 告诉我，最好的方法之一是识别设备试图收集的数据，然后向其提供垃圾版本。 柏林艺术家 Adam Harvey 在开发阻碍面部识别算法的化妆品和服装时就使用了这一策略。 Daniel Howe 和 Helen Nissenbaum 对名为 TrackMeNot 的浏览器插件做了类似的事情：该扩展程序不是隐藏用户的 Google 搜索，而是在后台不断运行自己的随机诱饵查询，因此用户实际搜索的任何内容都会迷失在虚假线索的海洋中。

人们也在音频领域尝试过这种技术。 波士顿大学研究隐私和监控的法学教授伍德罗·哈佐格 (Woodrow Hartzog) 告诉我，在他的法律职业生涯早期，他与辩护律师合作，他们担心他们与客户的监狱谈话会被记录。 为了反击，他们在后台播放了“胡言乱语磁带”——由 40 首不同口音的声音分层组成的音频文件。

2023年，南京大学研究员高明领导的团队利用人声以不同的方式击败了语音恢复算法。 它的干扰器名为 MicFrozen，由不想被录音的演讲者佩戴。 它会在他们说话时进行监听，然后根据说话者的声音生成实时超声波“反语音”流，就像耳机中的降噪技术一样。 然后，该设备发出另一层伪造的语音形状的声音，以误导任何试图重建丢失内容的算法。

巴拉达里的公司正在研发 Spectre I 设备，她不愿告诉我她的干扰器信号是如何工作的，但她说它们也类似于语音。 Spectre I 的发布视频声称该设备还能够检测附近麦克风的存在。 当我问巴拉达里将如何做到这一点时，她澄清说她的团队“目前仍在研究这部分内容”。

无论《Spectre I》的效果如何，录音军备竞赛都不会结束。 更强大的人工智能模型最终可能会部署一些自己的新聆听技巧。 他们可能会完全绕过录制的音频。 在斯坦利·库布里克的《2001：太空漫游》中，当两名宇航员退回隔音舱讨论断开 HAL 9000 的连接时，飞船上的计算机只是通过舷窗读取他们的嘴唇信息。 原则上，由经过足够对话镜头训练的模型驱动的可穿戴设备也可以做到同样的事情。 理论上，它还可以盯着两个人之间的一杯水，并从液体表面的振动中恢复他们的语言。

人工智能可穿戴设备可能总是比对抗措施更具优势。 毕竟，他们使用的技术是整个语音处理行业的产物，该行业需要数十亿美元的投资——不仅用于人工智能助理，还用于助听器、智能扬声器和电话会议工具。 与此同时，只有少数学者和小公司在保护我们免受这些技术的侵害。 “猫捉老鼠游戏的特点是，我们知道它们通常会如何落入老鼠手中，”哈佐格说。 “在这种情况下，这只猫包括一些有史以来最强大的公司。”

黑手党知道当一只老鼠是什么感觉。 当阿里洛塔这个有抱负的男人被告知穿上浴袍时，犯罪组织已经进行了数十年的监视军备竞赛。 执法部门开始窃听他们的电话后，老板们就会亲自处理业务。 有时，他们会使用安全屋或车辆，但这些也可能被窃听，因此敏感信息可能只能在边走边说的过程中传达。 最终，犯罪家族转向一次性手机，然后是加密设备。 但在这里，他们再次成为猫的牺牲品。

2018 年，FBI 开始秘密运营自己的加密电话公司 Anom。 通过线人，该公司销售了 12,000 台带有特殊 Anom 消息应用程序的设备。 黑手党家庭、摩托车团伙和其他犯罪组织的成员将手机视为身份象征，并用它们来谈判毒品交易、洗钱以及参与各种其他非法活动。 但他们提供的安全措施是一个诡计：他们发送的每条消息都被联邦政府拦截。
